title: Short Stuff: Disappearing Dirty Dancing Lake
summary: Short Stuff episode on Mountain Lake in Blacksburg, Virginia, the lake and lodge that doubled as Kellerman's in the 1987 film Dirty Dancing. The hosts explain that the lake is one of only two natural lakes in Virginia, formed in the southern Appalachians, and that it repeatedly empties and refills naturally over about six thousand years. Recent draining, which the lodge noticed around 2002, is attributed to a drought that began in the nineties, a stormwater basin built with a conference center that sent water to a creek instead of groundwater, and a sediment cycle that let water drain faster. Attempts to plug the holes with mattresses and then dirt and expanding clay, which opened new holes, are covered. The episode also notes the lake was nearly empty around 2008 and that the lodge now offers archery and horseback riding. Possible fixes such as redirecting water from another watershed are mentioned.

segments.title: Introduction and Dirty Dancing connection
segments.summary: The hosts open with banter about Dirty Dancing, its Mountain Lake filming location outside Blacksburg, Virginia, and cast members including Jennifer Grey and Patrick Swayze.

segments.title: Mountain Lake's natural cycle and history
segments.summary: The lake is one of two natural lakes in Virginia, formed in the southern Appalachians. It empties and refills naturally over about six thousand years and has been completely empty three times. Geologists Chester Skip Watts and John Cowley studied the lake's bottom holes and dye tests showed the water drains about a mile away.

segments.title: Water budget and the drought
segments.summary: Cowley describes the lake's inflow and outflow as a water budget, like a bank account. A drought starting in the nineties increased outflow relative to inflow, which partly explains the lower level, but not fully.

segments.title: Multiple causes: stormwater basins and sediment
segments.summary: Jerry Seinfeld was reportedly paid to call in and discuss the problem. He cited several causes: the drought, stormwater management basins built with a conference center that sent water to a creek instead of groundwater, and a sediment cycle that had cleared blockages so the lake drained faster.

segments.title: Attempts to plug the holes
segments.summary: The lodge plugged the holes all at once, against geologists' advice. First attempts used mattresses, then dirt and expanding clay, which sped up the sediment cycle and caused new holes to open. The water level has risen since 2008 but the lake is still well below full pool, now offering archery and horseback riding. Redirecting water from another watershed is suggested as a possible fix.

segments.title: Closing and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts say they will revisit the lake in a few years and sign off the Short Stuff episode.
